note: Follows 2.2 (levels, sublevels, orbitals) and sets up 2.4 (valence electrons, ions). Notation convention (PROVISIONAL until Matt confirms): filling order, e.g. [Ar] 4s^{2} 3d^{6}, written with true superscript runs ^{...}. Required through Kr (Z = 36), PROVISIONAL scope. Cr and Cu are the only exceptions taught. Every configuration and orbital diagram on these slides, and every configuration in the speaker notes, is checked by scripts/build_diagram_u02_s02.3_configurations.py. 50-minute period; the last 5 minutes are cleanup/reset.

fields.headline:
2.3
Electron
Configurations
fields.subhead: Write configurations and orbital diagrams through krypton, and catch mistakes in them.

imageSubjects.section: a long row of numbered wooden mail slots in a dim hallway, a few holding envelopes

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL scope: required through Kr (Z = 36), per the content brief; Matt to confirm. Period 5 and beyond (Mo, Ag, Au) are not taught on these slides and are not checked in the build script. PROVISIONAL notation: configurations are written in filling order, e.g. [Ar] 4s^2 3d^6, not energy order. Image prompt (section slot): a long row of numbered wooden mail slots in a dim hallway, a few holding envelopes.

fields.headline: Where Are Oxygen's Electrons?
fields.subhead: The periodic table gives you the count: 8. Today you write where each one sits.
fields.keyq: Oxygen has 8 electrons. Do all 8 have the same energy?

imageSubjects.concept: an apartment building at dusk with a few lit windows on different floors

slides.notes: Hook. Ask: do all 8 electrons have the same energy? Let them guess; the slides answer it (no). Z = 8 comes from the periodic table. Image prompt (concept slot): an apartment building at dusk with a few lit windows on different floors.

fields.headline: Reading an Electron Configuration
fields.subhead: Take 2p^{4} apart one piece at a time.
fields.k1_b:
2p^{4}

The big number in front is the level: 2.
fields.k2_b:
2p^{4}

The letter is the sublevel: p.
fields.k3_b:
2p^{4}

The raised number is the electron count: 4.
fields.mustwrite: A configuration lists where the electrons sit. Ground state means the lowest-energy arrangement.

imageSubjects.aside: a printed periodic table with oxygen's cell circled in pencil

slides.notes: Say it aloud: two-p-four. Level 2, p sublevel, 4 electrons. Ground state = lowest-energy arrangement; every configuration today is a ground state unless the slide says otherwise. Image prompt (aside slot): a printed periodic table with oxygen's cell circled in pencil.

fields.headline: The Order Electrons Fill In
fields.subhead: Read each arrow from top right to bottom left, then start the next arrow.
fields.a1_b: The lowest-energy open orbital fills first.
fields.a3_b: 4s fills before 3d, in K and Ca.

slides.notes: Walk each arrow top right to bottom left. We need the order through 5p: 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p. Say it as: 4s fills before 3d in neutral K and Ca. Do not say 4s is always lower than 3d (once 3d holds electrons it sits lower; that is S2.4, ions).

fields.headline: Pauli: Two per Orbital, Opposite Spins
fields.subhead: Up and down arrows are spin labels, not electrons orbiting opposite ways.
fields.a1_b: One orbital holds at most 2 electrons.
fields.a2_b: If there are two, their spins are opposite.
fields.a3_b: Two per orbital, not two per sublevel.

slides.notes: Spin up and down are labels, not literal rotation. Common mix-up: two per orbital, not two per sublevel (a p sublevel has 3 orbitals and holds 6).

fields.headline: Hund's Rule: Singles Before Pairs
fields.subhead: Equal-energy orbitals, like the three 2p boxes, each get one electron first.
fields.a1_b: Singles first, all pointing the same way.
fields.a2_b: Its 2p^{3} is three single electrons: 3 unpaired.

slides.notes: Figure: N in 2p. Correct = three singles, spins parallel. Wrong = one pair, one single, one empty box. Equal-energy orbitals are called degenerate. Electrons spread out first because sharing an orbital costs repulsion.

fields.headline: Reading an Orbital Diagram
fields.subhead: One box per orbital. Nitrogen has 7 electrons, so 7 arrows.
fields.a2_b: Draw the up arrow first in every box.
fields.a3_b: The raised number counts the arrows.

slides.notes: N has 7 electrons so 7 arrows: 2 + 2 + 3. Convention: draw the up arrow first in every box, and the label's raised number counts the arrows.

fields.headline: Filling Oxygen's 2p Boxes
fields.subhead: Four electrons, three boxes. Watch the order of the arrows.
fields.a1_b: The 2p sublevel has 3 boxes. Oxygen puts 4 electrons in them.
fields.a2_b: One up arrow in each box first.
fields.a3_b: The fourth arrow pairs up, pointing the opposite way.

slides.notes: Click build (see scripts/add_click_builds.py): the three 2p boxes fly in, then one arrow per click: up, up, up (Hund: singles first), then down in box 1 (Pauli: a pair has opposite spins). Result: 2p^4 with one pair and two singles, so 2 unpaired electrons. Have students draw each arrow in their notes at the same click. Same filling as the oxygen example later in this deck.

fields.headline: Writing a Configuration
fields.subhead: The same four steps, for every element.
fields.s1_b: Atomic number is the electron count.
fields.s4_b: The raised numbers must total Z.

imageSubjects.band: a periodic table wall chart photographed at a shallow angle

slides.notes: Four steps, every element. Caps: s 2, p 6, d 10, f 14. Always check that the sum equals Z. Image prompt (band slot): a periodic table wall chart photographed at a shallow angle.

fields.headline: Example: Oxygen
fields.subhead: Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: Write the longhand configuration and the orbital diagram for oxygen.
fields.g2_b:
Longhand configuration
Orbital diagram
Unpaired electrons
fields.mustwrite: Always check that the raised numbers add up to Z.

imageSubjects.aside: a small cylinder of oxygen gas with a regulator, on a lab cart

slides.notes: Students copy the setup; the work area stays empty on purpose and is filled live on the board. Answer on the next slide: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4, 2 unpaired. Image prompt (aside slot): a small cylinder of oxygen gas with a regulator, on a lab cart.

fields.headline: Oxygen, Worked
fields.subhead: Order first. Then singles before pairs in the 2p boxes.

slides.notes: Oxygen: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4, 2 + 2 + 4 = 8. The 2p boxes hold one pair and two singles, so 2 unpaired.

fields.headline: Example: Iron
fields.subhead: Configuration, orbital diagram, and the unpaired count.
fields.problem: Write the configuration for iron and draw its 4s and 3d orbital diagram. How many unpaired electrons?
fields.g2_b:
Longhand configuration
Orbital diagram
Unpaired electrons
fields.mustwrite: Fill 4s before 3d. We write 4s ahead of 3d.

imageSubjects.aside: a rusted iron nail on a white bench

slides.notes: Second orbital-diagram example, after oxygen. Students copy the setup, then work it; answer on the next slide. Fe, Z = 26. Fill 4s before 3d, and we write 4s ahead of 3d (filling-order notation, PROVISIONAL convention). Only the 4s and 3d boxes are drawn; the first 18 electrons (through 3p) are just counted. The [Ar] label on the next slide previews noble-gas shorthand, which has not been taught yet at this point: say 'the first 18 electrons, the same as argon' and let the shorthand slides name it. Image prompt (aside slot): a rusted iron nail on a white bench.

fields.headline: Iron, Worked
fields.subhead: The first 18 fill through 3p. Then 4s, then 3d.
fields.mustwrite: Fe ends 4s^{2} 3d^{6}: one pair and 4 singles in the 3d boxes.

slides.notes: Fe: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^6, written with the first 18 as [Ar] 4s^2 3d^6, 18 + 2 + 6 = 26. The 3d boxes hold one pair and four singles, so 4 unpaired. The 4s pair is drawn first, then the 3d boxes (Hund: one up arrow in each box, then pair). [Ar] here is a preview of the noble-gas shorthand taught two slides later; treat it as 'the first 18'.

fields.headline: Longhand: N, Cl, and Ca
fields.subhead: Calcium stops at 4s^{2}. The 3d sublevel stays empty until scandium.
fields.mustwrite: The raised numbers add up to the atomic number, every time.

imageSubjects.aside: period 3 of a periodic table wall chart, lit from the side

slides.notes: N: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3, 3 unpaired. Cl: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^5, 1 unpaired. Ca: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2, 0 unpaired. 3d stays empty until scandium. Image prompt (aside slot): period 3 of a periodic table wall chart, lit from the side.

fields.headline: Noble-Gas Shorthand
fields.subhead: Replace the filled inner core with a noble gas in brackets.
fields.mustwrite: Use the previous period's noble gas. Cl is in period 3, so its core is [Ne], not [Ar].

imageSubjects.concept: a neon sign tube glowing orange-red in a dark window

slides.notes: COMMON ERROR (brief): using the noble gas of the same period, or the element's own. Cl is period 3, so the core is [Ne], not [Ar]; the core is the previous period's noble gas. Shorthand: [Ne] 3s^2 3p^5, which equals the longhand 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^5. Next slide: the same idea for germanium, built one click at a time (the longhand first, then the noble gas before it in brackets). Image prompt (concept slot): a neon sign tube glowing orange-red in a dark window.

fields.headline: Shorthand: Germanium
fields.subhead: Write it long first. Then swap the argon part for [Ar].
fields.a2_b: [Ar] is a placeholder for argon's 18 electrons.
fields.a3_b: Then write what is left, the usual way.

slides.notes: Shorthand build for germanium (Z = 32), on text boxes, one per segment. The CLICK BUILD line at the end says exactly what each click does. Teach it in this order: write the longhand first; find the noble gas that comes BEFORE germanium and highlight those electrons; put that noble gas in brackets; finish the line. Longhand: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^10 4p^2, 2+2+6+2+6+2+10+2 = 32. The first five segments total 18 and are exactly argon's configuration, so [Ar] is a placeholder, a substitution like writing one symbol for a long repeated expression in math. Shorthand: [Ar] 4s^2 3d^10 4p^2, 18 + 2 + 10 + 2 = 32, with 2 unpaired electrons (the two 4p singles). Common error (brief): using the noble gas of the element's own period. Krypton ends germanium's period and comes AFTER it (Z = 36 > 32), so [Kr] would claim 36 electrons; the next slide shows the table strip. [Ar] sits against the remaining segments, in the space the highlighted block occupied, so the line reads [Ar] 4s^2 3d^10 4p^2 after click 3; click 4 writes the finished line as the answer to copy. Cl stays on the previous slide as the static example. A static export or print of this slide shows every shape at once (the highlight, the replaced segments and [Ar] overlap); for a handout use the --preview export of scripts/add_click_builds.py.

fields.headline: Why [Ar] and Not [Kr]?
fields.subhead: Germanium is in period 4. Its core is the noble gas that ends period 3.
fields.a1_b: Ends period 3. It comes BEFORE germanium.
fields.a2_b: Period 4, group 14. Use the previous period's noble gas.
fields.a3_b: Ends period 4. It comes AFTER germanium, so it is the wrong core.

slides.notes: Table strip, periods 3 and 4 (groups 1-2, 3-12 as spans, then 13-18). Argon (Z = 18) is the last element of period 3: the noble gas BEFORE germanium. Germanium (Z = 32) is period 4, group 14. Krypton (Z = 36) ends period 4: it comes AFTER germanium, so it cannot be a core for a 32-electron atom. Rule restated: the core is the previous period's noble gas. Positions are asserted from the atomic numbers in scripts/build_diagram_u02_s02.3_configurations.py. The marks use a tick, a cross and words as well as colour. Alt text on the picture describes the strip.

fields.headline: Example: Aluminum
fields.subhead: Notation only. No diagram this time.
fields.problem: Write the longhand configuration and the noble-gas shorthand for aluminum.
fields.mustwrite: Aluminum is period 3, so its core is [Ne].

imageSubjects.aside: a roll of aluminum foil partly unrolled on a white bench

slides.notes: Notation-only example: no orbital diagram. Students copy the setup, then work it. Answer on the next slide: Al, Z = 13, 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^1, 2+2+6+2+1 = 13; shorthand [Ne] 3s^2 3p^1, 10+2+1 = 13. Common error: [Ar] as the core. Argon (Z = 18) is bigger than aluminum's 13 electrons, so it cannot be a core. The core is the noble gas that ends the previous period (neon, period 2). Image prompt (aside slot): a roll of aluminum foil partly unrolled on a white bench.

fields.headline: Aluminum, Worked
fields.subhead: Longhand first. Then swap the first 10 for [Ne].
fields.mustwrite: Al is [Ne] 3s^{2} 3p^{1}, the same 13 electrons as the longhand.

slides.notes: Al: longhand 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^1, 2+2+6+2+1 = 13. Shorthand [Ne] 3s^2 3p^1: [Ne] stands for the first 10 (1s^2 2s^2 2p^6), then 10+2+1 = 13. Notation only; no diagram is drawn. If students use [Ar] as the core, have them add it: 18 + 2 + 1 = 21, not 13. Image prompt (data slot): the aluminum square of a periodic table wall chart, photographed close and slightly off-axis.

imageSubjects.data: the aluminum square of a periodic table wall chart, photographed close and slightly off-axis

fields.headline: Example: Bromine and Nickel
fields.subhead: Notation only. Two elements, one core.
fields.problem: Write the noble-gas shorthand for each element.
fields.mustwrite: Both are period 4, so the core is [Ar], never [Kr].

imageSubjects.aside: a nickel-plated metal bar and a sealed amber ampoule of bromine on a white tray

slides.notes: Notation-only example: no orbital diagram. Answers on the next slide. (a) Br, Z = 35: [Ar] 4s^2 3d^10 4p^5, 18+2+10+5 = 35. (b) Ni, Z = 28: [Ar] 4s^2 3d^8, 18+2+8 = 28. Common error: [Kr] because krypton is 'close' (Kr is Z = 36, one more than bromine, so [Kr] would already hold 36 electrons). Both are period 4, so the core is the noble gas that ends period 3, argon. Nickel follows the rules; the only exceptions taught are Cr and Cu. Image prompt (aside slot): a nickel-plated metal bar and a sealed amber ampoule of bromine on a white tray.

fields.headline: Bromine and Nickel, Worked
fields.subhead: Same [Ar] core. Then 4s, 3d, and 4p as needed.

slides.notes: (a) Br, Z = 35: [Ar] 4s^2 3d^10 4p^5, 18+2+10+5 = 35. (b) Ni, Z = 28: [Ar] 4s^2 3d^8, 18+2+8 = 28. Notation only; no diagram is drawn. Fill 4s before 3d, and write 4s ahead of 3d (filling-order notation, PROVISIONAL convention). Ni is not an exception. A student who writes [Kr] for either one has counted 36 electrons before writing anything else. Image prompt (data slot): the period 4 row of a periodic table wall chart, photographed close and slightly off-axis.

imageSubjects.data: the period 4 row of a periodic table wall chart, photographed close and slightly off-axis

fields.headline: Exception: Copper
fields.subhead: The rules predict 4s^{2} 3d^{9}. Watch what the real atom does.
fields.a1_b: Which sublevel loses an electron, and which gains one?
fields.a2_b: Copper and chromium are the only exceptions we learn.
fields.a3_b: 4s empties first in ions: Cu^{+} is [Ar] 3d^{10}, Cu^{2+} is [Ar] 3d^{9}.

slides.notes: Copper click build (the CLICK BUILD line at the end gives the clicks). Boxes for 4s and 3d only; the [Ar] core (18 electrons) is not drawn. Click 1: the atom as the rules predict, [Ar] 4s^2 3d^9 (4s before 3d; 18 + 2 + 9 = 29). Click 2: one 4s arrow leaves. Click 3: a 3d down arrow arrives in the fifth box. End: [Ar] 4s^1 3d^10, 18 + 1 + 10 = 29, one unpaired electron (the 4s). Same electron count before and after: an electron MOVES, none is gained. Say 'measured ground state', not 'textbook error'. The arrows are bookkeeping for the end state; the diagram does not track one electron's journey. Forward pointer to S2.4: the 4s^1 electron leaves first, so Cu^+ = [Ar] 3d^10 and Cu^2+ = [Ar] 3d^9 (both checked by the figure script). The reason follows on the Why slide. Do not extend this to Ag or Au: not taught, not checked (look it up).

fields.headline: Exception: Chromium
fields.subhead: Same move. The rules predict 4s^{2} 3d^{4}.
fields.a1_b: Count the arrows in 3d before and after.
fields.a2_b: Cr still has 24 electrons. [Ar] is 18, so 6 are drawn.
fields.a3_b: Count them at the end. Is it more than iron's 4?

slides.notes: Chromium click build. Click 1: predicted [Ar] 4s^2 3d^4 (18 + 2 + 4 = 24): four up arrows in 3d and one empty box. Click 2: one 4s arrow leaves. Click 3: an up arrow arrives in the fifth 3d box. End: [Ar] 4s^1 3d^5, 18 + 1 + 5 = 24; every box in 4s and 3d holds exactly one up arrow, all spins parallel (Hund), so 6 unpaired electrons, more than iron's 4. The arrows are bookkeeping for the end state: the arrow that leaves 4s is the down one and the arrow that arrives in 3d is an up one, so do not present it as one electron keeping its spin; the point is the final arrangement. Answer to the unpaired question: 6. Same teaching label as Cu: measured ground state. Mo (same group, one period down) is an exception too, and W is not; not taught, not checked here.

fields.headline: Why Cr and Cu Break the Pattern
fields.subhead: A simplified reason, and where it stops working.
fields.k1_b: 4s and 3d are almost the same energy, so a small change can tip the balance.
fields.k2_b: One 4s electron moves. 3d becomes completely full (Cu) or half full with parallel spins (Cr).
fields.k3_b: That lowers the atom's total energy slightly, so the real atom does it.
fields.mustwrite: A simplification, not a rule: it misses other exceptions. Learn Cr and Cu; look the rest up.

imageSubjects.aside: a coil of copper wire beside a chromium-plated tap on a lab bench

slides.notes: STUDENT LEVEL (simplified; say so out loud): 4s and 3d are very close in energy here. Moving one 4s electron gives a completely filled 3d (Cu) or a half-filled 3d with all five spins parallel (Cr). That lowers the atom's total energy slightly, so the real atom does that. This explains Cr and Cu; it does not predict every exception, and in this course students learn Cr and Cu and look the rest up. Do NOT say that half-full and full are always more stable. TEACHER LEVEL: the near-degeneracy of 4s and 3d is what lets a small energy change decide the arrangement. Textbook accounts cite exchange stabilization (same-spin electrons in different orbitals lower the energy; Cr has six parallel spins) and reduced electron-electron repulsion. PROVISIONAL: the textbook story is simpler than the real energy accounting, which needs electron-correlation calculations; that is why the heuristic fails. COUNTEREXAMPLES (checked against a secondary dataset, the mendeleev PyPI package, for Cr, Cu, Nb, Mo, W, Ag and Au; NIST was not reachable from here; still PROVISIONAL until Matt or a source confirms. The script itself checks only that the electron totals are 41 and 74): Nb is [Kr] 5s^1 4d^4, an exception that is not half-full or full; W is the regular [Xe] 6s^2 4f^14 5d^4 although Cr and Mo, in the same group, are exceptions. So the heuristic is not a predictor. Mo, Ag and Au (one period down) are not taught and not checked here. Forward pointer to S2.4: the 4s^1 electron leaves first, so Cu^+ = [Ar] 3d^10 and Cu^2+ = [Ar] 3d^9. Image prompt (aside slot): a coil of copper wire beside a chromium-plated tap on a lab bench.

fields.headline: Checking a Configuration
fields.subhead: Run these four checks in order.
fields.s1_b: Do the raised numbers add up to Z?
fields.s3_b: Singles first. Pairs have opposite spins.
fields.s4_b: Previous noble gas? Is it Cr or Cu?

imageSubjects.band: a teacher's red pen resting on a page of student work

slides.notes: Run the four checks in order: count, caps and order, Hund and Pauli, then core / Cr / Cu. Stop at the first failure. Image prompt (band slot): a teacher's red pen resting on a page of student work.

fields.headline: Example: Spot the Mistake
fields.subhead: Each was written as a ground state.
fields.problem: Each of these is wrong. Name the rule or fact it breaks.
fields.mustwrite: Add the electrons first. If the total is not Z, stop there.

imageSubjects.aside: a page of student work with a few lines circled in red pen

slides.notes: Answers on the next slide. Each was written as a ground state. (a) O: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 is 10 electrons, O has 8. (b) K: [Ar] 3d^1 puts 3d before 4s. (c) Ca: [Ne] 4s^2 is 12 electrons, wrong core. (d) Cr: [Ar] 4s^2 3d^4 obeys the rules but is not the real ground state. Replay the Chromium click build if students are unsure. Image prompt (aside slot): a page of student work with a few lines circled in red pen.

fields.headline: Spot the Mistake, Worked
fields.subhead: Four problems, four different checks. Each fix is on the right.
fields.f1_b:
(a) Count: 10, not 8
(b) Aufbau: 4s first
(c) Core: needs [Ar]
(d) Real Cr differs
fields.mustwrite: Cr follows the rules on paper, but the measured ground state is [Ar] 4s^{1} 3d^{5}.

imageSubjects.data: a pencil resting on a page of crossed-out electron counts

slides.notes: Corrected: (a) O 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4. (b) K [Ar] 4s^1. (c) Ca [Ar] 4s^2. (d) Cr [Ar] 4s^1 3d^5. (d) is the Chromium click build: predicted [Ar] 4s^2 3d^4, actual [Ar] 4s^1 3d^5. Teach 'rules-consistent' versus 'observed': (d) passes every rule on paper and is still not the real atom. Image prompt (data slot): a pencil resting on a page of crossed-out electron counts.

fields.headline: Example: Spot the Mistake, Diagrams
fields.subhead: Two orbital diagrams. Each breaks a different rule.
fields.a1_b: Only the three 2p boxes are drawn.
fields.a3_b: Name the broken rule. Redraw it correctly.

slides.notes: Orbital-diagram errors (brief items c, d), labelled (e) and (f) here. (e) N 2p drawn up, down, up: three singles but not parallel. (f) Ne 2s drawn up, up in one box: Pauli. Ask which rule each breaks and what the fix looks like.

fields.headline: Spot the Mistake, Diagrams, Worked
fields.subhead: One Hund error and one Pauli error. The fixes are drawn at left.
fields.f1_b:
(e) Hund: spins differ
(f) Pauli: same spin
fields.work:
Fixed:
(e) 2p: up, up, up
(f) 2s: up, down
fields.mustwrite: Hund: singles first, all spins the same. Pauli: two in one orbital must be opposite.

slides.notes: (e) Hund: unpaired electrons need parallel spins. Correct N 2p: up, up, up. (f) Pauli: two electrons in one orbital must have opposite spins. Correct Ne 2s: up, down. The brief's other Hund error (pair, single, empty) is the WRONG row on the Hund slide earlier in this deck.

fields.headline: Check Yourself
fields.subhead: Work all three in your notes before we compare.
fields.k2_b: Write the shorthand and sketch the 3p boxes.
fields.k3_b: Write the actual shorthand. Say why it is an exception.
fields.mustwrite: Show the electron sum for each one. If it is not Z, find the error.

imageSubjects.aside: a pencil and a blank sheet of lined paper on a lab bench

slides.notes: Answers (re-derived). P, Z = 15: 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^3, 2+2+6+2+3 = 15, 3 unpaired. S, Z = 16: [Ne] 3s^2 3p^4, 10+2+4 = 16; 3p boxes: one pair and two singles, 2 unpaired. Cu, Z = 29: [Ar] 4s^1 3d^10, 18+1+10 = 29. Exception: replay the Copper click build (slide 'Exception: Copper'): the rules predict [Ar] 4s^2 3d^9, one 4s electron moves into 3d, and the filled 3d lowers the atom's total energy slightly. That is the simplified reason from the Why slide (4s and 3d are close in energy); it does not predict every exception, so do not accept 'full is always more stable'. Image prompt (aside slot): a pencil and a blank sheet of lined paper on a lab bench.
